accuracy.evidence: Every grouping is unambiguous for a 5-8 year old: apple, banana and carrot are food and dog, frog and cow are animals; the odd ones out (car among fruit, chair among pets, bread among vehicles) have one clear shared property; strawberry and fire truck are both red and banana and taxi both yellow; antonym pairs big/small, hot/cold, fast/slow, up/down, open/shut, full/empty and stop/go match the CCSS L.K.5b examples. Near-synonym distractors (huge, warm, quick, high) are correctly labelled as nearly the same, not opposites.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-categorisation slips: grouping by appearance instead of kind (step 2 prediction 'cow is the biggest', 'all red' and 'all round' reasons, tag 'look'), believing an item can only ever belong to one group (step 3 prediction on strawberry and fire truck, m5), switching rule mid-sort (rule feedback 'The rule is colour', tag 'rule', m9), picking a near-synonym as an opposite (warm for hot, huge for big; tag 'same', p3, m2) and picking an associated word (sun for hot, door for open; tag 'goes', m3, m8).

lab_distinct.evidence: flag_sortw.js is built around a category rule: a basket sort where the current card is dragged into Animals or Food, an odd-one-out board, a rule switch where the same four cards are first sorted by colour and then re-sorted by kind with the baskets relabelled, a 'why together' reason picker, and an opposites matcher with near-synonym and associated-word decoys. No other flagship sorts one set under two rules or tests antonyms; it passed the 30% shingle gate against flagmeaning, flagnewword and the other young labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by doing it: sorting six cards shows a group is things of the same kind; the odd-one-out rounds force them to find the shared property; re-sorting the same cards under a new rule shows the rule decides the groups; the reason picker makes them name the rule; the opposites rounds show an opposite is the far end. Each done line states that idea in one sentence.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option: 'cow, it is the biggest' (size instead of kind; the board then shows the tree is the only non-animal), 'No, never: one is food' (the colour sort then puts strawberry and fire truck in Red together), and 'Warm' as the opposite of hot (the matcher then marks warm as only a little bit hot). Each is answered by the lab before the explanation.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions (odd one out, opposites of open and full, why bee, butterfly and bird go together, sorting a lemon by colour, farm animals vs pets) with every wrong answer tagged look, goes, same, rule or near, each giving a one-line reason that names the slip; the streak resets on a miss and the answer order rotates.

readability.evidence: Family audience, ages 5-8: kid text scores FK grade 0.8 with short sentences and concrete pictures (dog, apple, fire truck); adult text scores 8.3, within the 10.0 target. Canvas words are one or two words per card at 15-18px with a large emoji, and on-canvas questions are a single short line.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler and low overlap. Kid paragraphs each teach one move (group, odd one out, new rule, opposites); adult paragraphs cover why categories matter, the two habits, common mistakes with a 'be careful' note, and a one-sentence lab tour. Practice and mastery items each test a different card or pair.

mobile.evidence: walk.cjs passed on iPhone 13 and desktop; per-step element screenshots at 390px (light) and 1200px (dark) show the large picture cards, two half-width baskets, full-width young-mode buttons and no clipped labels. The current card sits alone at the top so a short downward drag reaches either basket.

accessibility.evidence: axe returned zero WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light and dark themes on desktop and phone. Every drag has a button equivalent with an aria-label (Put the frog in Animals, Is the car the odd one out?), the canvas aria-label reads the current question and feedback, and colour is never the only cue (check tags, 'odd one out' and 'big ↔ small' labels).

sources: Common Core State Standards ELA, Language L.K.5a (sort common objects into categories) and L.K.5b (relate frequently occurring verbs and adjectives to their opposites)
Common Core State Standards ELA, Language L.1.5a (sort words into categories, e.g. colours, clothing, to gain a sense of the concepts)
